questions.q: What does the Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO) actually measure?
options: The percentage of trades that lost money in the backtest
The fraction of in-sample/out-of-sample combinations where the configuration that won in-sample turns out to be a below-median out-of-sample performer
The total number of strategy configurations tested
The correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample returns
questions.explain: PBO uses combinatorially symmetric cross-validation to split performance history into many IS/OOS combinations, then measures how often the in-sample-best configuration ends up a below-median performer out-of-sample. A high PBO indicates the selection process is picking up overfitting noise.

questions.q: What method is combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV) most structurally similar to, as covered earlier in this chapter?
options: Plain KFold with shuffle=True
Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation (CPCV) from Lesson 16
StandardScaler normalization
GaussianMixture regime detection
questions.explain: CSCV is a CPCV-like construction: it splits performance history into subsamples and symmetrically combines them into in-sample and out-of-sample sets across every combination, similar in spirit to CPCV's combinatorial approach to validation.

questions.q: According to the minimum backtest length heuristic, what should happen as the number of strategy configurations tested increases?
options: The required backtest history to trust a high Sharpe ratio should also increase
The required backtest history should decrease, since more trials average out noise
The Sharpe ratio threshold for success should be lowered
No adjustment is needed regardless of how many configurations are tested
questions.explain: Because the expected maximum Sharpe ratio across many trials rises with the number of trials (Lesson 17's DSR logic), more strategy configurations tested requires a longer backtest history before a high in-sample Sharpe ratio can be trusted.

questions.q: What is 'backtest decay,' and why is it considered a strong red flag for overfitting?
options: A technical bug where backtest code becomes slower over time
A strong backtested Sharpe ratio that erodes toward zero or worse once the strategy meets live or paper-traded data
The gradual loss of historical data due to storage limits
A requirement to re-run the backtest every quarter
questions.explain: Backtest decay describes a strategy performing well in the backtest but deteriorating once it faces genuinely new, live data — essentially overfitting revealing itself once it meets information it was never fit to.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed in the lesson as a practical mitigation against backtest overfitting?
options: Holding out a slice of data untouched until the very end of the research process
Preferring simpler models with fewer free parameters
Writing down the hypothesis and configuration before running the test
Testing as many parameter combinations as possible to maximize the in-sample Sharpe ratio
questions.explain: Maximizing in-sample Sharpe ratio by testing as many combinations as possible is the problem the lesson warns against, not a mitigation. Mitigations include untouched holdouts, fewer parameters, pre-registered hypotheses, and running CPCV/DSR before trusting results.
